doc.title: Lisa Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 22, 2021

title: Moving to New York and being an original voice
summary: She came in 1993, returned in 1995, felt at home, and Clifford Barbaro hired her because she sounded like no one else.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. So you get to New York for lessons. Had you intended to go back at that point, to Australia?

So I came in ’93 for nine months and did study. I hadn’t intended to come back at the end of nine months. I had visa issues, it’s a long story I’m not going to go into, I was actually sort of forced out. That’s a long story. We won’t go there. And then I just saved up money, spent a year and a half in Australia and then came back permanently in ’95. When I came back in ’95 I knew, well New York and the vibe in New York, I felt at home. I didn’t feel like a freak. Even though I had such great supportive musicians and I discovered myself musically in Australia, just culturally New York supported someone like me. I felt like, and I wondered because of my biggest hero being Bernie McGann I used to sound a lot like — I think I still have a lot of Bernie in me. I went to every one of his gigs for a whole year when I first moved to Sydney. He was playing about three times a week. It was fantastic. But always wondering if the way I play was only valid in Australia. That’s what I didn’t know, it was like I’ve gotten accolades for being an original voice in Australia. I didn’t know if it would work anywhere else. So I remember going to like my first couple of jam sessions in the East Village, in ’93, and a couple of people coming up to me and giving me advice. And I was sort of taken aback because I wasn’t really getting that in Australia. And I realized it was coming from a place of, we like what you’re doing, you need some advice. You know if someone just says, “Yeah you sound great.” That means nothing to you. But if someone is saying hey have you ever checked out such-and-such and such-and-such? I reckon you could check that out. Or something like that, that’s what it was like. And also I realized, and I got my first gigs with Clifford Barbaro the drummer. And we had a regular gig. And after doing it for like

a month I asked him, “Why did you pick me? I hear all these — such great musicians everywhere, why did you pick me to be in your band?” He’s like, “You don’t sound like anybody else. And that was the penny dropping through the maze, like, ah, there’s always room for another original voice in this music. And that’s what’s taken me, that’s given me a career actually, because I don’t sound like anyone else. And it doesn’t mean that — I definitely have influences. You can hear some Ornette, you can hear Bernie McGann, on bari you can hear Gerry Mulligan. You can hear these influences but at the same time I feel like it was really great that when I was really young I made up my own way of doing things.
